transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-21 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jenna Liu (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (NimbleHealth Dir of ML), Tom Alvarez (NimbleHealth SRE), Liam O'Connor (Product Owner)

Summary:
Quick review of last week's microburst mitigation, current TTFT spike in streaming mode, and a plan to run a 6k sample with prefix caching + streaming on. Decide kernel path A vs B for seq-len distribution.

Topics:
- TTFT variances after enabling streaming
- Sequence length bucket behavior (16/64/256+)
- Kernel selection and hedge policy
- KV/prefix cache hit-rate effect
- Next steps and access for benchmark runner

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription may contain errors) ---
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for making the time. quick check in — we'll run through the numbers Jenna pushed yesterday and then decide the next set of experiments. how's everyone?
[00:22] Priya: hi, good, yes — we're seeing that weird 2nd minute bump in TTFT when streaming is enabled, so that's the main thing we wanna root cause.
[00:35] Jenna: right, so the microbench we ran — to be clear — streaming on + no prefix cache gave average TTFT 220ms but 95th jumped to 720ms on some traces, and a few microbursts push to 1.2s which is bad for our user flows.
[00:50] Tom: those 1.2 seconds are exactly the ones hitting seq-length 256 in our sim, it's like an interaction between the kernel selection and the batcher.
[01:10] Samir: ok. quick taxonomy — when we say "streaming" here we mean chunked token flush with early websocket frames, right? not the Redwood "fastpath" short-circuit.
[01:22] Jenna: yep, chunked frames so we can show first tokens early. the fastpath is a different runtime optimization.
[01:30] Liam: just to be explicit, our SLA for search suggestions is 300ms 95th ideally. so those 720/1.2s spikes are outside the target.
[01:45] Priya: and a lot of the prod traffic is short prompts but with occasional long completions because of our multi-turn context. so the distribution has a fat tail.
[02:05] Jenna: that's why we suggested sequence-bucket A/B testing — run the same workload across kernel A (vectorized attention path) vs kernel B (memory-optimized path) and see which gives better tail.
[02:26] Tom: question — are kernel A/B deterministic across different batch sizes? previously we saw kernel selection flip at runtime based on sequence length and batch composition which muddied analysis.
[02:40] Jenna: yes it's policy-driven. for the microbenchmark we'll pin a kernel using the runtime override so we can isolate. that's part of the plan.
[02:52] Samir: perfect. can you summarise the items you need from them?
[03:00] Jenna: we need the prod token dist CSV (counts per seq-len bucket), the representative prompt templates, and an allowlist for staging runner IPs.
[03:12] Priya: we'll send the token distribution and prompt categories. the IP allowlist, Tom will handle.
[03:19] Tom: yep, I'll open the staging VPC and paste the bastion details.
[03:30] Samir: great. next— the 6k sample. Jenna, you said you could run that with prefix-caching and streaming on?
[03:38] Jenna: yep. streaming + prefix caching + simulated KV hit-rates at 50/75/90 percent. we'll try three runs.
[03:47] Priya: wait — the KV sim, is that per-request or global?
[03:51] Jenna: per-request probabilistic hit simulation so it approximates realistic reuse. not perfect but enough to see trends.
[04:00] Liam: and also include a run where we enable light quantization? I know quant tends to help throughput but might affect single token latency.
[04:10] Jenna: we can do a quantized run but isolated; we won't mix quant with the kernel A/B in the same sweep to keep variables separated.
[04:20] Samir: and we'll capture TTFT, 50/95/99, and early byte streaming frame times. also log kernel switch events and batch sizes.
[04:32] Priya: ok. any concerns on data residency or logs? we need audit logs for the bench run.
[04:38] Samir: yes Redwood will enable limited audit trails for the staging experiment; logs will be stored in the pilot bucket with retention 30 days. we'll share the link.
[04:50] Tom: perfect. now about multiplication of kernel paths — Jenna, last week you mentioned hedging policies, like fallback to the less-latent kernel when the fastpath misses. can you expand?
[05:05] Jenna: sure, it's basically runtime hedging: if we detect the batch composition is likely to trigger a high latency kernel, we can route those requests to a different worker type or preemptively choose kernel B which is more stable for long sequences. there's an amortized cost increase but improves 95/99.
[05:24] Liam: is that something we can toggle per-route? our product team wants it only for suggestion route, not for bulk generation.
[05:31] Jenna: yes per-route policies are supported — route-level kernel hints and fallback tiers.
[05:38] Priya: bandaid question: could we just reduce max tokens to avoid 256+? that changes UX though.
[05:44] Samir: that is a blunt instrument; doable but not ideal. better to tune kernel/hedge and caching first.
[05:53] Priya: agreed. let's try the less-intrusive path first.
[06:00] Samir: ok. technical check — Tom, do you have capacity to run the sample locally if we hand off a runner?
[06:07] Tom: yes we can host the runner in staging, but we need the SSH allowlist and the runner image.
[06:13] Jenna: we'll send the runner image and a one-click script. should be multiple-cloud friendly.
[06:20] Priya: please make sure the script emits per-token timestamps — we need to map prior UX traces to these runs.
[06:28] Jenna: will do.
[06:30] Samir: on the measurement side, we also want to capture tail queue wait times inside the batcher, because sometimes the batcher defers a single request for microseconds to fill a batch and that adds to TTFT.
[06:43] Tom: we can add that metric to the runner.
[06:46] Liam: side note — competitor Megaburst AI claimed they could hold 95th under 300ms using aggressive quant in their blog; are we worried about that?
[06:56] Samir: we mentioned them earlier; benchmarking's the only way to know. our focus is predictable tradeoffs.
[07:05] Priya: ok. anything else on streaming framing? we noticed some partial frames arriving double in the browser during spikes. could be client buffer.
[07:15] Tom: we saw that too, and it's not on the server-side logs. probably the websocket client batching. we'll triage separately — not blocking the kernel analysis.
[07:25] Jenna: back to experiments: proposed matrix — 3 KV hit rates x 2 kernel pins x streaming on/off x seq-buckets; that'll be roughly 18 core runs and ~6k requests each.
[07:39] Priya: timeline for results?
[07:42] Jenna: we can start runner 11/22, finish runs by 11/24, and publish a summary by 11/24 EOD.
[07:50] Samir: good. Priya, any internal stakeholders to loop in for the kernel decision meeting?
[07:55] Priya: include infra lead and product; I'll invite Sasha and Marco.
[08:02] Samir: noted.
[08:05] (longer section: detailed numbers review — Jenna reads results from yesterday's microbench)
[08:05] Jenna: ok reading: run 1 baseline (no stream, no cache) TTFT mean 190ms p95 460ms p99 810ms — run 2 streaming on TTFT mean 220ms p95 720ms p99 1.2s — the difference correlates with increased batch fragmentation.
[08:37] Tom: batch fragmentation meaning smaller batches because streaming flushes earlier?
[08:40] Jenna: exactly — the sooner you flush, the less opportunity to coalesce tokens into a full bigger batch.
[08:45] Priya: but sometimes streaming actually improves perceived latency even if backend TTFT is higher, because the UI shows early partial tokens. we need both metrics.
[08:55] Samir: we'll capture both early-frame and full-response times.
[09:00] Liam: can the runtime do partial KV-cache priming to avoid misses on the first streaming frame?
[09:06] Jenna: there is a priming trick — prefix warm-up on request arrival, but it costs CPU. we can try a light warm-up in the pilot.
[09:14] Priya: let's include a run with prefix warm-up at 10ms budget.
[09:19] Jenna: noted.
[09:22] Samir: operational question — any legal/PII concerns with sending token distributions?
[09:26] Priya: distribution is aggregated counts, no PII, safe.
[09:30] Tom: security wise the staging bucket will be inside their VPC. we asked for limited access.
[09:36] Samir: Redwood will provide the audit link and will redact raw prompts if necessary; we'll clarify in the email.
[09:44] (middle of call — some cross talk and clarifications)
[09:44] Jenna: one more measurement: we should log kernel flip frequency per request ID so we know how often the runtime changes kernels mid-request.
[09:54] Tom: that's interesting — we had a case where kernel flipped between attention paths and that aligned with a 90ms pause.
[10:02] Samir: ok. anything else?
[10:05] Priya: what about cost — if we hedge to a more expensive worker to reduce tail, how big is the uplift?
[10:12] Jenna: approximate uplift is 8-15% for hedging in our sims, depends on utilization. we'll quantify in the next note.
[10:20] Liam: we may be comfortable with small uplift if it stabilizes SLA.
[10:24] Samir: fair. last items — schedule and deliverables: runner start 11/22, raw logs by 11/24, kernel decision 11/26.
[10:34] Priya: agreed. Samir, can you send a single email summarizing access, the runs, and what we'll need?
[10:40] Samir: yes I'll send a summary + the benchmark sheet link (internal): https://redwood.app/bench/nimble-6k
[10:48] Tom: we'll respond with bastion details.
[10:50] (wrap-up)
[10:50] Jenna: action items: I'll run the A/B kernels and attach logs, Samir will send pricing delta, Priya and Tom will share data and access.
[10:58] Priya: thanks everyone.
[11:00] Samir: thanks, we'll talk after the runs. bye.

End of call.
